Intro
In the last post we went through three rounds of feature work, and we also left a bug in on purpose: the
code
index
delete bug.
So today we're talking about the Vibe Coding debugging workflow: from spotting a bug, to guiding the AI to fix it, to regression-testing it and committing.
Of course, you might be thinking: AI is so smart these days, how would we even run into bugs?
Actually, you'd be wrong. No matter how smart or capable the AI is, if you don't review its work and don't try to understand it, you're going to run into exactly this.

the-worst-way-to-report-a-bug
The worst way to report a bug
First, I want to talk about the bug reports I run into most often in my own dev work. They usually look like this:
ul
li
"Delete is broken."
"The screen won't move."
"I clicked the button and nothing happened."
When I get one of these, as an engineer, a few thoughts flash through my head right away:
What exactly is broken about delete?
What do you mean the screen won't move? It won't update, or it won't navigate?
Did nothing happen because you didn't fill in a field so the button was disabled, or did it really do nothing?

Then I try it myself and it works fine, so I go dig through the code looking for clues. When I still can't find anything, all I can do is tell the person who reported it: "It works fine on my end, can you try again?" And then we go back and forth like that a bunch of times.

The same thing applies to AI. The AI also needs enough information from you to fix the problem. If you don't give it enough, it's stuck doing what a human engineer would do: wildly guessing at possible causes and reading tons of code (burning through a lot of Tokens). Then you start complaining that the AI is dumb and slow, when really the root cause is that "you never described the problem clearly in the first place."
https://images.israynotarray.com/blog/ai/ithome-2026-vibe-coding/Codex%20%E5%9C%96%E5%83%8F%202026%E5%B9%B49%E6%9C%8823%E6%97%A5%20%E4%B8%8A%E5%8D%8811_15_09.png

It has no way of knowing what you did, what the flow was, what you saw, or what you expected. So it guesses blindly and forces a change, and you end up spending a lot of time verifying it over and over.
At that point, how is that any different from playing Minesweeper?
So next I'm going to give you a formula and a workflow, so you can explain things to the AI precisely, verify the fix, and get bugs fixed fast.

Just because you reviewed it doesn't mean there are no bugs. It just means the scenarios you tested happened not to have any.
That's exactly why so many engineers ask you for more information. So stop blaming engineers for being slow at debugging.

where-to-look-for-clues-the-console-or-a-screenshot
Where to look for clues: the console or a screenshot
A lot of the time, a bug doesn't show up on the screen at all. So what do you do then?

First you need to be clear about what you're building, since different kinds of projects have different ways of handling this. Our practice expense tracker app is a Web App, so we can open the browser's developer tools and check the error messages in the
Console
. Those messages usually tell you what's wrong. Opening it is easy:
Windows / Linux:
macOS:
Cmd + Option + I
Then just switch to the "Console" tab and you'll see the error messages.

Handling them is simple too: copy the whole thing and paste it to the AI. Don't translate it, summarize it, or come up with your own explanation, because the parts you think don't matter are often the key. Just handing it straight to the AI is the fastest way.
Where the Console tab is in the browser's developer tools (for bugs that show red error text)
https://images.israynotarray.com/blog/ai/ithome-2026-vibe-coding/20260803114546.png

Some of the errors in the screenshot above come from browser extensions. So if you see a lot of red text in the console, try turning your extensions off and testing again (or use an incognito window). That helps you avoid chasing the wrong thing.

Next up is the second kind: bugs that are hard to describe in words (layout out of whack, wrong colors, inconsistent text sizes, and so on). For these, I recommend taking a screenshot, dragging it straight into the AI's input box, and then following the same debugging workflow. That saves you a lot of time writing descriptions.
Of course, if you can describe it clearly, that's still best.
the-fix-isnt-the-end-regression-test-it-the-same-way
The fix isn't the end: regression-test it the same way

No matter what, when the AI tells you it's fixed it, everything's fine, or it's all done, that doesn't mean you're off the hook. It just means it's handing things back to you, because you're the owner of this project.
When you review, take out those same steps to reproduce and walk through them again yourself:

There's a bug in the delete feature. Steps to reproduce:
1. Starting with no data, add yesterday's lunch for 120, category Food
2. Then add today's drink for 60, category Food
3. The list is sorted newest to oldest:
  - Today's drink
  - Yesterday's lunch
4. I click the "lunch" entry to open the edit form, then I just press delete and confirm

Expected result this time: the edit form shows lunch's 120, and after deleting, lunch disappears and the drink is still there.
Expected result this time: the edit form shows lunch's 120, and after deleting, lunch disappears and the drink is still there.

Check it again by following the exact steps you originally reported to the AI. You do want to know whether it actually fixed the bug you gave it, right? Don't just call it done because the AI said it's fixed.

On top of that, you also need to check that the old features didn't break, since the part that just changed might affect other places. So this is when you go through the old features too and make sure they still work.
Remember a few ground rules:
The AI saying "I fixed it" doesn't count. It only counts once you've checked it yourself.
Whether old features got broken is also something you have to confirm yourself.
Only when all of that checks out is it actually "fixed." At this point you can tell the AI:
I've reviewed it. The original bug is gone, the old features aren't broken, and the known TODOs are all gone. Please commit.
And with that, you've gone through one full round of the Vibe Coding debugging workflow. The same workflow applies whether you're working with human engineers or AI.
when-it-just-wont-get-fixed-three-fallbacks
When it just won't get fixed: three fallbacks
Next I want to share a scenario people don't talk about much: when you've gone back and forth several times and the AI still can't fix it.
In that situation, doing nothing isn't an option. Instead, you should have a few fallbacks ready. Here are three you can use:
Ask from a different angle

: Don't keep repeating useless descriptions like "it's still broken." Try it a few more times and give the AI what you newly noticed, for example... "deleting the first entry works, deleting the second one goes wrong." Sometimes a new clue helps find the problem.
Narrow it down

: First have the AI verify the data flow. Tell it to ignore the screen for now and show you the data before and after the delete. Split the problem into data and screen. The screen is usually driven by the data, so the screen only means something once you've confirmed the data is right.
Restore a single file with git

: After going back and forth with the AI several times, ask it to restore things to the last commit. Every feature commit you made was saved for exactly this moment. Have the AI list which files were changed first, look them over before you say yes, and only restore the one file that's broken, instead of wiping out all the progress you worked hard on today.
All three fallbacks are telling you one thing:
AI doesn't nail every bug fix or feature on the first try. The people who plan their fallbacks are the ones who go the distance.
So, putting the whole thing together, the workflow looks like this:

Wrapping up
By now you should have a pretty good handle on the debugging process, so let's wrap up with a quick summary.
When you're Vibe Coding, don't panic when you hit a problem. Follow this workflow:
Describe it with the debugging trio: steps to reproduce, expected, actual. If there's red text, paste all of it; if it's a visual problem, send a screenshot.
Turn on Plan Mode and let it diagnose the problem before it touches anything.
Review the fix yourself: the original bug is really gone and no old features got broken. Only commit once it passes.
If it won't get fixed, use the three fallbacks: ask from a different angle, narrow it down, and restore only the specific file.
Tomorrow we'll do something more fun: let the numbers do the talking by adding a stats page and a pie chart to the app.
Hopefully this post makes fixing bugs feel a little less like a lottery. See you tomorrow on Day 13.
